summary: Sets out basic requirements for authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA) of SIP sessions, needed as SIP services are deployed on the Internet. It describes the need rather than a solution. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Phone companies must know who is calling, if they are allowed, and how much to charge. This lists what the Internet phone system must support so those three jobs can be done.

questions: what are aaa requirements for sip
how does sip authenticate users across domains
how do prepaid sip services work
subtitle: What SIP networks must do to check who you are, whether you can call, and what to bill

tldr.problem: As SIP (the protocol for Internet phone calls) began deployment on the Internet, networks needed to authenticate users, authorize their calls, and track usage for billing. No standard interface existed for SIP systems to talk to authentication and accounting servers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out baseline requirements for an interface between SIP servers and AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) servers. It describes what data must be transferred, when, and how decisions get made—such as allowing a user to call only through a specific proxy or checking credit before placing a call.
tldr.outcome: This document provides a requirements checklist for protocol designers. Solutions like Diameter and XML-based protocols can be built to meet these requirements. The RFC itself does not design the protocol; it establishes what any solution must handle.

facts.label: Excluded SIP requests
facts.value: CANCEL and ACK for non-2xx responses (proxy-generated)

today: RFC 3702 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It established the requirements that later AAA protocols like Diameter have implemented for SIP networks. It remains the reference for what SIP AAA interfaces must support.

sections.title: The Three Jobs of a Phone Network
sections.content:
When SIP sessions begin on the Internet, the network must do three things:

  • Authentication means proving who the caller really is, usually with a password or certificate.
  • Authorization means deciding whether the caller is allowed to do what they asked, like calling a particular number or using a particular service.
  • Accounting means tracking what happened so the network can bill for it, analyze usage trends, or audit activity.

These are abbreviated AAA. In traditional phone networks, the home network of a user maintains this information locally. On the Internet, SIP servers need to query AAA servers (specialized systems that hold user profiles and permissions). This RFC describes what the interface between SIP servers and AAA servers must support.
sections.eli5: Three things happen when you make a call: the system checks you are who you say you are, it checks you are allowed to do what you asked, and it writes down what you did so it can charge you.

sections.title: Basic Requirements All AAA Systems Must Meet
sections.content:
The RFC outlines requirements that any AAA solution for SIP must meet. First, a SIP proxy must be able to ask an AAA server in its own domain, in a different domain, or through intermediary proxies. Second, the system should be able to figure out which AAA server to query just from the information in the SIP message. Third, the interface must be access-independent: whether users connect over WiFi, broadband, mobile, or wired Internet, the AAA interface works the same way.

The AAA server must be able to update what the SIP server knows about a user, tell the SIP server when a session changes in ways that matter (like adding a video stream), and ensure secure, reliable delivery of messages. Importantly, adding AAA checks should not make call setup slow, especially for ongoing sessions where latency is critical.
sections.eli5: The system must work between networks, not add delay to real calls, and let servers ask questions and get reliable answers back.

sections.title: Proving Who You Are
sections.content:
The AAA system must authenticate users based on any SIP request, except for CANCEL and ACK messages that proxies generate (those do not carry user credentials). The authentication mechanism should be flexible enough to work with any method that SIP itself supports, such as Digest authentication (similar to HTTP authentication).

The RFC does not specify how authentication happens; it only requires that the AAA interface be flexible enough to accommodate whatever SIP chooses. This allows the interface to adapt as new authentication methods emerge.
sections.eli5: When a user sends a message to call someone, the AAA server must check their password or certificate. Different ways of checking must all be supported.

sections.title: Deciding What You Can Do
sections.content:
Authorization means checking what a user is allowed to do. The AAA interface must let servers authorize any SIP request and also transfer rich information to guide the decision—for instance, the server might say: "This user can call, but only if the request goes through Proxy C."

Users can be de-authorized (told they can no longer do something, even mid-call) and re-authorized (told their permission is refreshed). The system must support credit control: checking whether a prepaid account has enough credit before executing a chargeable event, like placing an international call.

These features enable service providers to apply flexible policies—for instance, cutting off a user whose account is overdue, or allowing a call only if routed through a specific proxy for logging.
sections.eli5: The system must say what each user is allowed to do, sometimes with conditions. It must also let the network decide to stop letting someone do something mid-call, or remind it that permission is still okay.

sections.title: Tracking What Happened
sections.content:
Accounting collects data about what happened. The RFC requires the ability to separate accounting information by different aspects: for instance, tracking "session duration" separately from "3-way calling service". The system must report events tied to session lifecycle (like when the call starts and stops) and also one-time events (like an instant message unrelated to any session).

The system must support both immediate one-time accounting records (e.g., a payment cleared) and session-based records (START when the call begins, INTERIM updates during the call, STOP when it ends). It should track usage per media type (voice accounting separate from video). The AAA server can configure parameters for when and how accounting records are generated.

For systems that correlate billing across multiple networks, the accounting interface must be able to include arbitrary identifiers (like a call ID) so records can be tied together later.
sections.eli5: The system must write down what happened: when calls started and stopped, what media was used, and enough detail to charge correctly and know what went on.

sections.title: Example Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC includes two concrete scenarios. The first is a roaming user: User A is away from home but uses his home network's authentication server to make a call through a proxy provider. The proxy checks with the home AAA server, which confirms the user's identity and allows the call, then the proxy sends accounting data back to the home network for billing.

The second scenario is conditional authorization: User A's home AAA server tells the proxy that the user's calls must be routed through a specific second proxy (for example, one that offers call logging). The first proxy uses SIP loose-routing to ensure the call traverses the required second proxy before reaching its destination.

These examples show how AAA enables flexible, multi-domain SIP deployments where users can roam, different networks can cooperate, and service providers can enforce policies.
sections.eli5: A traveler calls home through a provider, and the home network checks and charges correctly. Or a network requires certain calls to go through a logging proxy first.
